name: LuaJIT Remake (Deegen)
baseline: PUC-Rio Lua 5.1 interpreter (also compared against the LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter)
workload: Geometric mean over the repo's luabench Lua programs (fannkuch, nbody, spectral-norm, binary-trees, deltablue, richards, json, havlak, scimark and others), run through run_bench.sh pinned to one core, GC disabled in every implementation.
claimed_speedup: Interpreter is 185% faster than the official PUC Lua 5.1 interpreter and 34.6% faster than the LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter (README, geometric mean). Deegen paper abstract, via search snippet only: interpreter 179% faster than PUC Lua and 31% faster than the LuaJIT 2.1 interpreter; baseline JIT 360% faster than PUC Lua and 33% slower than LuaJIT's optimizing JIT, faster than LuaJIT on 13 of 44 benchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: clang/clang++ -O3 release build via ljr-build in Docker (from CMakeLists.txt); build flags of the PUC Lua and LuaJIT baselines are not stated
hardware: Intel i7-12700H laptop, 32GB DDR4, benchmarks pinned with taskset (README footnote)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 semantics only; x86-64 Linux only; garbage collector not implemented; package library (require, module) missing; the Lua table is rebuilt on hidden classes; build needs Docker and a custom LLVM-based generator toolchain; the interpreter is generated from a bytecode semantics description (Deegen) rather than hand-written.
caveats: Work in progress and not production-ready per the README. Garbage collection was turned off for every implementation in the comparison, which hides the collector cost of PUC Lua and LuaJIT. README names no PUC Lua or LuaJIT versions or their build flags. Single laptop; run_bench.sh notes thermal fluctuation of about 10 percent. The JIT tiers are not finished in the repo (README says ongoing; last commit is 2025-02-18), so the JIT numbers exist only in the paper. The paper (Deegen: A JIT-Capable VM Generator for Dynamic Languages, OOPSLA 2026 per the search result) could not be opened because arXiv is blocked.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Deegen JIT-capable VM generator for dynamic languages LuaJIT Remake faster than PUC Lua' (paper and repo README)

name: LuaJIT
workload: kostya/benchmarks: brainfuck interpreter bench.b and primes (sieve of Atkin plus trie), Lua 5.4.7 against LuaJIT 2.1. plb2: nqueen, matmul, sudoku, bedcov, LuaJIT 2.1 against QuickJS.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks README (UPDATE 2026-07-19): bench.b 5.686 s for LuaJIT vs 37.051 s for Lua 5.4.7 (about 6.5x, derived from page data); primes 0.309 s vs 1.056 s (about 3.4x, derived from page data). plb2 README (see caveats for URL): LuaJIT 2.1 nqueen 5.31 s vs QuickJS 59.04 s, matmul 2.66 vs 135.66, sudoku 4.48 vs 67.55, bedcov 10.52 vs 37.56.
compiler_and_flags: kostya: Debian forky/sid Docker image with clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.1.0 installed; build flags of Lua 5.4.7 and LuaJIT 2.1.1748495995 not stated in the README. plb2: prebuilt LuaJIT 2.1 (JIT) and QuickJS 23-12-09.
hardware: kostya: Intel Xeon E-2324G; plb2: Apple M1 MacBook Pro
stars_or_usage: 5.8k stars (GitHub mirror of the upstream repository)
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 language level with some 5.2 extensions, so no Lua 5.3/5.4 integers, utf8 library or goto-era features beyond that; the JIT is not allowed on some platforms (iOS, consoles), where only the interpreter runs; ports to x86, x64, ARM, ARM64, PPC, MIPS; JIT warm-up cost.
caveats: Both suites are independent of the LuaJIT project, but compile flags are not stated. The speedup holds for loop and numeric heavy code; allocation or string heavy code is not covered by the rows quoted. Interpreter-only LuaJIT (-joff) is about 2.3x slower than JIT mode in Rochus Keller's Are-we-fast-yet run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rochus-keller/Are-we-fast-yet/HEAD/Luau/Results.pdf, 2025-10-25, i5-8350U, gcc 12.2.0). The plb2 numbers are at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/attractivechaos/plb2/HEAD/README.md (Apple M1; LuaJIT 2.1 and QuickJS 23-12-09 versions given). The arXiv paper 'The Green Side of the Lua' (2601.16670) reports LuaJIT 2.0.4 about 7x faster and 7x lower energy than Lua 5.4.7, from a search snippet only because arXiv is blocked.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Lua VM interpreter optimization paper 2025 speedup over Lua 5.4 geometric mean open source implementation C++' (surfaced 'The Green Side of the Lua'); numbers from kostya/benchmarks and attractivechaos/plb2 READMEs

name: QuickJS
baseline: Duktape 2.3.0 (also compared with XS 8.8.0, MuJS 1.0.6, JerryScript, Hermes 0.1.0 and V8 in the same table)
workload: bench-v8 version 7 scores (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes); higher is better; all engines run as interpreters.
claimed_speedup: Total score 942 for QuickJS vs 408 for Duktape (about 2.3x, derived from page data). Per test QuickJS vs Duktape: Richards 777 vs 218, DeltaBlue 761 vs 266, Crypto 1061 vs 202, RayTrace 915 vs 484, EarleyBoyer 1417 vs 620, RegExp 251 vs 156, Splay 1641 vs 1389, NavierStokes 1856 vs 1003.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9.2 on Fedora 21; QuickJS 2019-07-09 qjs x86 64-bit -O2; Duktape 2.3.0 duk x86 64-bit -O2
tradeoffs: Executable 620K vs 331K for Duktape on the same page; supports recent ECMAScript (ES2020 and later) and a bignum extension; reference counting with a cycle collector; interpreter only, no JIT.
caveats: Numbers are from 2019 (QuickJS 2019-07-09, Duktape 2.3.0) and run by QuickJS's own author. The page opened is a Chinese-language mirror of the author's benchmark page (quickjs-zh/QuickJS bench.md); the original on bellard.org was not opened. The bench-v8 sources the page says ship in tests/bench-v8 are in the release archive but are not in the current GitHub tree (404 at HEAD), so the harness is reproducible from the release tarball only.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Hermes vs QuickJS benchmark comparison faster startup interpreter embedded JavaScript engine github' (result: quickjs-zh/QuickJS bench.md)

name: XS JavaScript engine (Moddable SDK)
workload: bench-v8 version 7 scores in Bellard's QuickJS benchmark table (RegExp disabled for XS because the engine could not run it); higher is better.
claimed_speedup: Total score without RegExp 738 for XS 8.8.0 vs 468 for Duktape 2.3.0 (about 1.6x, derived from page data). Per test XS vs Duktape: Richards 444 vs 218, DeltaBlue 553 vs 266, Crypto 408 vs 202, RayTrace 1156 vs 484, EarleyBoyer 1175 vs 620. Duktape is faster on Splay (1389 vs 1048) and NavierStokes (1003 vs 836).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9.2 on Fedora 21; XS 8.8.0 xst x86 64-bit -O3; Duktape 2.3.0 -O2
license: GPL-3.0 / LGPL-3.0 / Apache-2.0 / CC-BY-4.0 combination per the SDK README (commercial licence also offered)
tradeoffs: Targets microcontrollers (README: devices with about 45 KB free RAM); executable 1.2M vs 331K for Duktape in the table; multi-licence SDK, so check which licence applies to the XS sources you copy.
caveats: Benchmark was run by the QuickJS author in 2019 on XS 8.8.0, a much older version than today's; XS lost two of seven tests and could not run RegExp. The XS engine lives under xs/ inside the Moddable SDK repository. First-party performance claims by Moddable were not found.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Hermes vs QuickJS benchmark comparison faster startup interpreter embedded JavaScript engine github' (result: quickjs-zh/QuickJS bench.md)

name: Hermes
workload: KusStar/benchmark-static-hermes: calc.js, json.js, md5.js and nbody.js execution time only (precompile and engine start-up excluded), bytecode Hermes (main branch) against QuickJS built with its Makefile.
claimed_speedup: Bytecode Hermes vs QuickJS: calc.js 2085 ms vs 6101 ms, md5.js 2027 ms vs 3381 ms, nbody.js 841 ms vs 1150 ms, json.js 648 ms vs a QuickJS timeout. Bellard's 2019 bench-v8 table (Hermes 0.1.0 binary, -O): total 968 vs 942 for QuickJS vs 408 for Duktape.
compiler_and_flags: Hermes: cmake -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for the main and static_h branches; QuickJS: plain make; compiler not named (macOS only harness)
tradeoffs: Executable 27M vs 620K for QuickJS in Bellard's table; built for React Native with precompiled bytecode and startup in mind; Hermes releases are tied to a specific React Native version per the README.
caveats: Third-party harness, macOS only, QuickJS version not stated. The Hermes advantage is large on calc.js and small elsewhere; Bellard's own 2019 numbers show Hermes about level with QuickJS (968 vs 942). Start-up latency, Hermes's headline claim, is excluded from these timings. The static typed Hermes row (calc.js 4 ms) runs typed code and is not comparable.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Hermes vs QuickJS benchmark comparison faster startup interpreter embedded JavaScript engine github' (result: KusStar/benchmark-static-hermes README)

name: PrimJS
workload: Octane benchmark suite (version 9 score and 15 sub-benchmarks) on PrimJS vs QuickJS.
claimed_speedup: Octane score 3735 vs 2904 for QuickJS (about 28% higher). Per test: RayTrace 2751 vs 1273, EarleyBoyer 4270 vs 2284, NavierStokes 4166 vs 2640, PdfJS 6642 vs 4236, Crypto 1844 vs 1349; PrimJS is slightly lower on CodeLoad (16992 vs 18137) and MandreelLatency (9587 vs 9680).
compiler_and_flags: gn args: is_debug=false, enable_optimize_with_O2=true, target_cpu arm64, target_os mac; compiler not named; PrimJS defaults enable_primjs_snapshot, enable_compatible_mm and enable_tracing_gc left on; QuickJS build arguments not stated separately
license: Apache-2.0 (with MIT and BSD-3-Clause components per the README)
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; engine of the Lynx cross-platform framework
tradeoffs: Template interpreter with stack caching, tracing garbage collector instead of QuickJS reference counting, ES2019 level, Chrome DevTools Protocol debugger, initial WebAssembly support; gn-based build tied to the Lynx tree.
caveats: First-party numbers, one machine, one suite; compiler name and the QuickJS build arguments are not stated, which is the only gap to tier A. QuickJS is pinned to an older commit (6e2e68) and the table does not give its date.
found_via: WebSearch: 'JavaScript interpreter "faster than QuickJS" Octane speedup open source engine paper embedded'

name: Pallene
baseline: PUC-Rio Lua interpreter (version used in the paper not confirmed)
workload: Statically typed Pallene modules compiled ahead of time to C against the same programs in Lua; the repo benchmarks directory holds binarytrees, binsearch, centroid, conway, fannkuchredux, fasta, mandelbrot, matmul, nbody, objmandelbrot, queen, sieve and spectralnorm.
claimed_speedup: Paper (SBLP 2018, Science of Computer Programming 2020), from search snippets only: running time reduced by 20% to 60% on some benchmarks and about five times faster than Lua on others, with array and arithmetic benchmarks (sieve) similar to LuaJIT; no number was confirmed on an opened page and the snippets disagree on the magnitude.
tradeoffs: Statically typed, ahead-of-time compiled sister language of Lua (README); output is a C extension module, so a C compiler is needed at build time and the code is loaded through require; it is a companion for hot paths, not a replacement interpreter.
caveats: Numbers are snippet only because the paper hosts (inf.puc-rio.br, ScienceDirect, ACM) and an independent blog comparison by Elmar Klausmeier (2020) are blocked; the README gives no figures; the Lua version, compiler flags and hardware of the paper are unknown. Peer-reviewed paper exists, so a retier to B is possible once it can be read.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Pallene statically typed companion language for Lua paper benchmark speedup over Lua'

name: yklua (Yk JIT retrofitted into PUC Lua)
language: C (Lua interpreter) with the Rust Yk JIT
baseline: PUC-Rio reference Lua interpreter (the interpreter yklua is built from)
workload: Lua benchmark set run with the Yk meta-tracing JIT enabled vs the unmodified interpreter; a Mandelbrot benchmark is the headline example.
claimed_speedup: Geometric mean of about 2x across a wider set of Lua benchmarks; Mandelbrot 3.2 s down to 0.8 s (about 4x); about 400 lines added and under 50 changed in PUC Lua (all from search snippets of Laurence Tratt's 2026 blog post and talk; not verified on an opened page).
tradeoffs: Needs the Yk JIT built separately (README); marked experimental; the README says the test suite is currently failing for non-serialised compilation; tracks upstream PUC Lua instead of being stuck at Lua 5.1 like LuaJIT.
caveats: Snippet only: the blog (tratt.net) is blocked and the repo README and PR #157 carry no numbers. No LICENSE file was found at the repo root (raw LICENSE returned 404); the code derives from PUC Lua (MIT) but the licence is unconfirmed, hence usability reference. The same source says yklua does not reach LuaJIT's peak performance.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Yk meta-tracing JIT retrofitted Lua interpreter yklua speedup paper'

name: LuaAOT (lua-aot-5.4)
workload: Lua modules compiled by the luaot compiler to C (bytecode converted into C functions with gotos, no bytecode dispatch) against the standard interpreter running the same Lua; README says numerical benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: 'For numerical benchmarks it can be twice as fast as regular Lua. But overall, it is not as fast as LuaJIT or Pallene.' (README)
compiler_and_flags: README recommends compiling the generated C with at least gcc -O2; no benchmark flags stated
tradeoffs: Modified Lua 5.4.3 interpreter plus the luaot compiler; each Lua module becomes a C file that must be compiled into a shared object and require-d; the interpreter must be the matching modified build.
caveats: README gives a single qualitative figure (twice as fast on numerical programs) with no tables, hardware or benchmark list. It accompanies the paper 'A Surprisingly Simple Lua Compiler' (SBLP 2021, ACM), which could not be opened. Research prototype.
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight Lua interpreter faster than PUC Lua 5.4 github benchmark README "faster than" Lua 5.4 embeddable VM C++'

name: Wren
baseline: Lua 5.2.3 (also LuaJIT 2.0.2 with the JIT disabled, Ruby 2.0.0, Python 2.7.5 and 3.3.4)
workload: Method call, DeltaBlue, binary trees and recursive Fibonacci microbenchmarks from test/benchmark, best of ten runs, interpreter start-up excluded.
claimed_speedup: Method call: Wren 0.12 s vs Lua 0.35 s and LuaJIT -joff 0.16 s. Binary trees: Wren 0.22 s vs Lua 0.52 s (LuaJIT -joff 0.11 s is faster). Recursive Fibonacci: Wren 0.20 s vs Lua 0.28 s (LuaJIT -joff 0.10 s is faster). DeltaBlue has no Lua row.
hardware: MacBook Pro 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7, 16 GB 1600 MHz DDR3
tradeoffs: Class-based concurrent scripting language with its own syntax (Smalltalk, Lua and Erlang influences), not a Lua drop-in; small VM (README: under 4,000 semicolons); fibers instead of Lua coroutines.
caveats: Numbers are from the early 2014 era on one laptop, against Lua 5.2.3 (not 5.4); compiler and flags not stated; the author notes LuaJIT with the JIT enabled is much faster than every engine in the chart. Benchmark programs are public in test/benchmark.
found_via: WebSearch: 'embeddable scripting language implementation paper faster than Lua' (surfaced Wren as a Lua competitor); numbers from doc/site/performance.markdown in the repo

name: libriscv
baseline: LuaJIT 2.1 and Luau interpreter (call overhead also compared with wasm3 and wasmtime)
workload: Game-scripting microbenchmarks (200x1200 samples, call overhead subtracted): function call and syscall overhead, integer and float math, fib(40), Taylor series, sieve of 10M, memcpy and memset, RISC-V guest code in libriscv against Lua code in LuaJIT or Luau.
claimed_speedup: Luau gist (https://gist.github.com/fwsGonzo/5ac8f4d8ca84e97b0c527aec76a86fe9): call overhead 2 ns vs 87 ns, integer math 3 ns vs 38 ns, fib(40) 220 ns vs 489 ns, sieve(10M) 138 ms vs 574 ms. LuaJIT gist (https://gist.github.com/fwsGonzo/1af5b2a9b4f38c1f3d3074d78acdf609, AMD Ryzen 7 6860Z): call overhead 3 ns vs 196 ns, integer math 3 ns vs 85 ns, sieve(10M) 225 ms vs 241 ms; LuaJIT wins fib(40) (101 ns vs 167 ns) and naive memcpy (117 ns vs 1222 ns).
hardware: LuaJIT gist: AMD Ryzen 7 6860Z (ThinkPad Z13); Luau gist states no CPU
tradeoffs: Scripts are RISC-V programs built with a RISC-V C/C++ toolchain, so the scripting language is C, C++ or Rust compiled to RISC-V, not a dynamic language; sandboxed emulator with per-instance memory limits and about 20k lines of code; binary translation and libtcc options exist for more speed.
caveats: First-party gists with no compiler, flags, Luau version or libriscv mode (interpreter or binary translation) stated; the README says benchmarks are hand-picked for game-engine scripting. Not a like-for-like comparison, since libriscv runs ahead-of-time compiled guest code while Lua runs interpreted or JIT-compiled scripts. Mixed results against LuaJIT on compute-heavy rows.
found_via: WebSearch: 'embeddable scripting language implementation paper faster than Lua' follow-up; found via github.com/fwsGonzo/libriscv README benchmark links

name: Luau
workload: Interpreter dispatch, bytecode design and runtime tuning; no benchmark workload is described on the performance page.
claimed_speedup: No numbers: the performance guide says the interpreter is 'noticeably faster than Lua 5.x (including Lua 5.4 which made some of the changes similar to Luau, but doesn't come close)' and can match the LuaJIT interpreter on some workloads.
tradeoffs: Lua 5.1 derived dialect with gradual typing, a separate bytecode compiler, vector type, sandboxing features and an optional x64/arm64 JIT; not fully compatible with newer Lua versions.
caveats: Claim is qualitative and first-party. Rochus Keller's Are-we-fast-yet run (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rochus-keller/Are-we-fast-yet/HEAD/Luau/Results.pdf, 2025-10-25, i5-8350U, gcc 12.2.0, Luau make config=release) has no PUC Lua row: Luau default measured 2.39x slower than LuaJIT default in geometric mean, about level with LuaJIT -joff (2.32x), and 1.64x with Luau codegen.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Luau performance interpreter faster than Lua 5.1 5.4 benchmark results Roblox'

name: pocketpy
baseline: CPython 3.8.10 (README also lists Lua 5.3.3 and C++ gnu++11 in the same table)
workload: Primes benchmark (benchmarks/primes.py) on pkpy 1.2.7 against CPython 3.8.10, Lua 5.3.3 and C++.
claimed_speedup: Primes: pkpy 2.385 s vs CPython 3.8.10 2.871 s (about 1.2x, derived from page data); Lua 5.3.3 took 1.576 s and C++ 0.104 s. README also says pkpy is currently as fast as CPython 3.9.
tradeoffs: Portable Python 3.x interpreter in C11 with no dependencies beyond the C standard library, aimed at game scripting as an alternative to Lua; a subset of Python with its own C API.
caveats: Does not beat the in-list baseline: in its own table Lua 5.3.3 is about 1.5x faster than pkpy. Win over CPython is small, on one benchmark, and measured with pkpy 1.2.7 (the README version), not the current release. Compiler and flags not stated. Listed to document the shortcoming.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com pocketpy README while checking embeddable Python/Lua alternatives
